slides.title: Making it fair
slides.oldHtml:
Making it fair

Five temperatures, 10–80 °C
Keep all other variables the same
Control: boiled amylase
Repeat 3–5 times; take the mean
Plot temperature (x) against time (y)
slides.newHtml:
Making it fair

  • Test 5 temperatures: 10–80 °C
  • Keep pH, volumes & concentrations the same
  • Control: boiled amylase (denatured)
  • Repeat 3–5 times and take the mean
Shorter time to clear starch → faster rate (rate = 1 ÷ time)

Whiteboards: When water boils at 100 °C, what is broken?
ACovalent bonds between H and O atoms
BWeak intermolecular forces between H₂O molecules
CIonic bonds between H⁺ and O²⁻ ions
⚠ EXAMINER TRAP: NEVER say covalent bonds break on boiling!

slides.title: Giant covalent structures
slides.oldHtml:
Giant covalent structures

Millions of non-metal atoms joined by strong covalent bonds
  • Like a giant ionic lattice, but with no charged ions
  • Very high melting & boiling points (lots of energy to break bonds)
  • Insoluble in water — no conduction (except graphite)
Why is Carbon so good at this?
Carbon (Group 4) has 4 outer electrons → forms up to 4 strong covalent bonds in every direction to build giant networks! (Silicon does too, e.g. quartz SiO₂.)
1 carbon → 4 strong covalent bonds → endless 3D network
Quartz (SiO₂) — giant covalent too
slides.newHtml:
Giant covalent structures

Millions of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds
  • Giant lattice — no charged ions
  • Very high m.p. & b.p. — many strong bonds to break
  • Insoluble — no conduction (except graphite)
Why Carbon?
Group 4 → 4 outer electrons → forms 4 strong covalent bonds in every direction! (Silicon too: quartz SiO₂)
1 carbon → 4 strong covalent bonds → endless 3D network
Quartz (SiO₂) — giant covalent too

slides.title: Mini-whiteboard: Which carbon?
slides.newHtml:
Mini-whiteboard: Which carbon?

Diamond
Graphite
C60
1. Extremely hard — 4 strong bonds per carbon
→ Diamond
2. Conducts electricity — delocalised electrons
→ Graphite
3. Hollow ball of 60 atoms — simple molecule
→ C60 fullerene
4. Soft & slippery — weak forces between layers
→ Graphite
